teaser: Monet set up his easel on a station platform and painted the one thing nobody can hold: steam.
review_notes:
Third Impressionist exhibition, April 1877, in an apartment at 6 rue Le Peletier rented by Caillebotte: check address and the number of station views shown (usually given as seven or eight; lesson says 'at least seven').
Caillebotte paying the rent of Monet's small studio near the station (rue Moncey): widely reported, check.
The story of Monet persuading the station director to hold trains and stoke engines comes from Jean Renoir's memoir of his father and is presented as a story, not as fact.
Zola's review is paraphrased, not quoted.
Canvas size about 60 x 80 cm.
Find block: the figure standing on top of a rail car at left is read from the image; it is a few strokes.

lesson.text: This canvas was painted with one room in mind. In April 1877 the Impressionists held their third group show in a rented apartment on rue Le Peletier in Paris. Monet did not send one picture of a train station. He sent at least seven, meant to be seen together, wall after wall of the same smoky hall.

The hall was the Gare Saint-Lazare, the busiest station in Paris. Trains left from here for Rouen and Le Havre, the Normandy coast where Monet grew up, and for Argenteuil, where he lived. He had passed under this roof hundreds of times as a commuter. In January 1877 he came back with canvases.
Monet could not afford to work in Paris that winter. His friend Gustave Caillebotte, a painter with family money, paid the rent on a small studio a few minutes’ walk from the platforms.

So what do you paint in a train station? Not really the trains. The engine here is a dark shape, almost a silhouette. What fills the canvas is everything the engine throws into the air, and Monet noticed that it does not all look alike.

lesson.title: Three kinds of vapor
lesson.text: Follow the smoke from the open air into the shed. It changes color as it goes.

spots.title: White steam
spots.text: Out in the daylight, steam is thick white paint, laid on in curls. It stands out against the pale sky and the dark freight cars below it.

spots.title: Blue smoke
spots.text: Under the roof the same vapor turns blue and gray. It is in shadow now, and it blurs the iron beams until you can hardly tell roof from cloud.

spots.title: The engine
spots.text: The locomotive is a few strokes of near black with a tall chimney. Monet gives it less detail than the air around it.

lesson.text: White in the sun, blue in the shade: the steam is a way of showing light itself. That was the real subject. A critic at the time, the novelist Émile Zola, wrote that you could hear the trains rumbling in these pictures, and that modern painters had to find poetry in stations the way their fathers found it in forests.

For all its haze, the picture stands on a very firm frame. The station had been rebuilt in the 1860s with huge sheds of iron and glass, the newest architecture in the city. Monet uses that structure like the beams of a stage set.
Three simple lines hold the fog in place.

lines.label: The iron tent
lines.text: The edge of the roof rises to a peak and falls again, like a gable. Everything bright in the picture sits inside this triangle of open sky.

lines.label: The gas lamp
lines.text: One thin vertical, a green lamppost, stands near the middle. It gives your eye a fixed point to measure the drifting steam against.

lines.label: Platform level
lines.text: Wagons, engine and crowd all line up along one low band. Above it is two thirds of the canvas, left to roof, smoke and light.

lesson.text: Two thirds of the painting, then, is air. This was the daring part. Earlier painters of railways, when they painted them at all, showed machines and engineering. Monet shows weather indoors.

A story told by the painter Renoir’s son says Monet put on his best suit, called on the station director, and introduced himself grandly as “the painter Claude Monet.” Trains were supposedly held and engines stoked so he could have his smoke.
People are here too, though you have to hunt for them. Monet reduces travelers to quick dark dashes, the way you see strangers when you hurry through a station yourself.
Most figures stand on the ground. One is perched above everybody else, on top of a rail car. Can you spot him?

spots.title: The man on the wagon
spots.text: A railway worker stands on the roof of a car, drawn with four or five strokes, his head just reaching the white steam. No face, no hands, and yet you read him at once.

lesson.text: That worker took Monet seconds to paint. The whole canvas, about 60 by 80 centimeters (roughly 24 by 31 inches), was worked fast, partly on the spot, among porters and passengers. The paint of the ground is so thin in places that the weave of the canvas shows through.

Painting in a crowd like this was only possible because of a small invention from 1841: the metal paint tube. Before it, oil colors were kept in pig bladders that dried out and burst, and painters mostly stayed in the studio.
Monet painted the Gare Saint-Lazare twelve times in a few months, changing the spot and the light each time. It was his first real series, years before the haystacks and the cathedrals.

spots.title: The crowd
spots.text: On the right platform, passengers are a row of dark dabs with a few touches of red. The crowd is treated as one mass, like the steam.

spots.title: Lamp glass
spots.text: The lantern on its post is painted pale green and white, a small cool echo of the glass roof above.

spots.title: Two men on the tracks
spots.text: Two figures stand in the foreground at left, built from a handful of vertical strokes. Their size tells you how vast the shed is.

spots.title: Glass and iron
spots.text: The roof panels are strokes of blue, green and white laid side by side. Daylight comes through them and falls in pale patches on the ground.

spots.title: The city beyond
spots.text: Through the open end of the shed, the buildings of Paris dissolve into light blue. The station opens straight onto the city.

spots.title: Signed and dated
spots.text: “Claude Monet 77” in dark paint at the lower left: the year he spent the winter on these platforms.

lesson.text: After that spring he never painted Paris again in any sustained way. He followed the Normandy line out of this station instead, toward Vétheuil, the coast, and finally Giverny. In a sense the train in this picture is the one that carried him off.

quiz.question: Where were Monet’s station paintings first shown?
options: At the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877
quiz.explanation: He sent at least seven station views to the Impressionists’ third group show in April 1877.

quiz.question: Who paid for Monet’s studio near the station?
quiz.explanation: Caillebotte, a fellow painter with family money, covered the rent.

quiz.question: Why is the steam white on the left and blue under the roof?
options: Two different engines burn different coal
Monet ran out of white paint
One is in sunlight, the other in shade
quiz.explanation: The vapor takes the color of the light it is in, which is what Monet wanted to show.

quiz.question: How many times did Monet paint the Gare Saint-Lazare?
quiz.explanation: Twelve canvases in a few months, his first real series.

quiz.question: What invention of 1841 made painting in such a place practical?
quiz.explanation: Tubes replaced fragile pig bladders and let painters carry oil colors anywhere.

facts.text: The locomotive is the most detailed part of the painting.
facts.explanation: It is a dark silhouette; the steam and light get far more attention.

facts.text: About two thirds of the canvas shows roof, smoke and light rather than trains or people.
facts.explanation: Wagons, engine and crowd all sit in one low band along the platform.

facts.text: The Gare Saint-Lazare series came after Monet’s haystacks and cathedrals.
facts.explanation: The station pictures of 1877 came first, years before those later series.
